source.title: Challenging BIG-Bench Tasks and Whether Chain-of-Thought Can Solve Them
source.authors: M. Suzgun; Nathan Scales; Nathanael Schärli; Sebastian Gehrmann; Yi Tay; Hyung Won Chung; A. Chowdhery; Quoc V. Le; Ed H. Chi; Denny Zhou; Jason Wei

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. Some appendix prompt sections are abbreviated or blank, but this does not prevent assessing the reported results relevant to the claim.
record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream task accuracy across model scales, rather than measuring held-out pretraining loss or fitting scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper’s discussion of pretraining scaling laws is background and cites other work, so it is not recorded as a result. Results comparing answer-only and chain-of-thought prompting are included here only where they report scale-dependent downstream performance. Most scale-curve values are plotted rather than stated numerically.
record.test_reason: The paper plots its own few-shot BBH accuracy against model scale for InstructGPT, Codex and PaLM, with and without CoT. This bears on V6 (downstream performance vs scale) in a new setting. It fits no scaling law and reports no pretraining loss, so V1–V5 and V7 are not tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that answer-only prompting underestimates model capabilities. With CoT, Codex beats the average human rater on 17/23 BBH tasks and PaLM 540B on 10/23. CoT gains need sufficient scale and can unlock emergent performance on some tasks with flat scaling curves, though not all (e.g. Causal Judgement).
record.recipe_differences: Evaluates few-shot downstream benchmark accuracy across model scales, using answer-only and manually written CoT prompts; it does not fit held-out pretraining-loss scaling laws or optimize compute allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: The effect of CoT varies with model scale and task; the paper reports no CoT improvement on Causal Judgement.

fits_no_version.finding: The benefit of CoT prompting is negative or zero in small models and grows with scale in all three families.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gains from reasoning-style prompting emerge only above a model-scale threshold.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Scale-curve values are mostly presented in figures rather than stated numerically, and no uncertainty estimates are reported. The authors caution that human-rater scores and task results should be interpreted carefully because the human evaluation was not fully representative and some task descriptions were difficult to follow.
record.rows_left_out: The paper includes per-task accuracy comparisons for several model families in Table 3 and many per-task scale plots in Appendix B. These do not all report scale-dependent outcomes in text; only the aggregate scale results and task-specific patterns explicitly described as evidence about scale were retained.

untested.parts: Predictability of downstream performance from pretraining loss, and any quantitative fit or extrapolation of downstream accuracy vs scale.
All: text-only downstream evaluation, no power-law fits.

missing.what: Answer-only (no-CoT) aggregate BBH scaling curves per family, as a separate scale-vs-accuracy result from the CoT curves

Per-task scale curves for all 23 tasks across three families. Several show flat or non-monotonic curves, e.g. Ruin Names and Snarks, where CoT lags answer-only in all three families. rows_left_out mentions these but does not record them.
missing.locator: Appendix B, Figures 8–13; Section 5 failure analysis

record.verdict_notes: Evidence for V6 is weak in precision. All scale results are figure-only with no uncertainty. OpenAI model sizes are unknown (footnote 3), so scale is ordinal by model name. The Codex scale labels contain a duplication error. The emergent, flat-then-jump curves argue against 'predictable' improvement on individual tasks, even though the aggregate rises.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation of pretraining-loss power laws from small runs to much larger runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation at fixed compute.
Effects of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream accuracy across model scale on BBH, but not whether downstream performance is predictable from pretraining loss or across a broad set of downstream tasks.
Does not compare fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocations across fitting choices, nor test whether pretraining-loss curves bend.

rows.subject: InstructGPT models (text-ada-001 through text-davinci-002)

rows.operation_detail: Compared average BBH accuracy across model scales with and without chain-of-thought prompting.
rows.measure: BBH accuracy and CoT-minus-answer-only performance as model scale increases
rows.baseline: Answer-only curve and random-performance reference; figure only
rows.value: CoT gain is negative or zero for text-ada-001 through text-curie-002, then the CoT-versus-no-CoT delta increases with scale up to the largest model; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The text explicitly describes the trend, but does not provide numerical values for the curve.
rows.check: For V6 the relevant result is CoT accuracy rising with scale. Text says the CoT-minus-no-CoT delta grows up to the largest model, and it is negative or zero at a-1 to c-1. Values are figure only. OpenAI model sizes are undisclosed (footnote 3), so the scale axis is ordinal.

rows.size_stated: Several model scales; exact parameter counts not stated
rows.operation_detail: Measured task accuracy across model scales with answer-only and CoT prompting.

relationships.condition: Aggregate BBH accuracy (23-task average) with CoT across InstructGPT, Codex and PaLM scales
relationships.reason: The text reports accuracy improving with larger models in all three families (R1–R3). Values are figure only.
relationships.display_finding: Aggregate chain-of-thought accuracy increased with model size in all three families.

relationships.condition: Multi-Step Arithmetic, Tracking Shuffled Objects and Web of Lies on OpenAI models
relationships.reason: Without CoT the scaling curve is flat. With CoT, performance jumps from about random only at the largest scales (emergent), so improvement depends on prompting and is not smooth (R4–R6).
relationships.display_finding: Performance stays flat without chain-of-thought prompting, while chain-of-thought produces a jump from approximately random performance only at the largest scales.

relationships.reason: The authors describe a flat scaling curve, with 57.8% answer-only vs 50% random and no gain from CoT (R7).
relationships.display_finding: The scaling curve was flat, with answer-only accuracy of 57.8% versus 50% random performance and no gain from chain-of-thought prompting.
